title: India and China Can Build a Multipolar World, Says Economist Jeffrey Sachs
excerpt: The Columbia economist told India Today that within 25 years, India and China will be the world's two largest economies, and that closer cooperation between them could anchor a genuinely multilateral order.
body:
• Economist Jeffrey Sachs says India and China will be the world's two largest economies within a quarter-century, with the US falling to third — and India the largest at some point this century.
  • In an India Today interview ahead of the BRICS summit in Delhi, Sachs called the India-China relationship "the most important bilateral relationship in the world."
  • He argued stronger India-China cooperation on trade, investment, technology and supply chains could anchor a genuinely multipolar world order.
  • Sachs credited a BRICS joint declaration in Delhi with reaffirming support for multipolarity and UN reform, while sharply criticizing US unilateralism.

US economist Jeffrey Sachs has predicted that India will become the world's largest economy at some point this century, telling India Today that within less than a quarter-century, India and China will rank as the world's two largest economies with the United States in third place. The remarks came in an interview given ahead of the BRICS summit in Delhi, where the bloc issued a joint declaration reaffirming its support for a multipolar world order and reforms to the United Nations.

Sachs, a Columbia University professor and one of the world's most widely cited development economists, said stronger cooperation between New Delhi and Beijing could create a multilateral order no longer dominated by Washington. "India and China together can really make a multilateral world," he said, adding that China has an interest in India's economic success because it would help build that multipolar framework.

The world's most important bilateral relationship

Sachs described the India-China relationship as "the most important bilateral relationship in the world," arguing that deeper cooperation between the two countries would have far-reaching consequences for global trade, investment, technology partnerships and supply chains. He acknowledged that border tensions persist between the two countries but maintained that economic partnership would still accelerate India's growth.

"India's growing the fastest of all the large countries right now and foreign investment from China in all kinds of joint ventures would accelerate that even more," Sachs said. He pointed to demographics as a structural tailwind: China's declining population and India's expanding one, he argued, make it likely that India joins China in the top two global economies within 25 years.

"I'm looking at the time just in less than a quarter century now when India and China will be the two largest economies in the world. The United States will be third at that point. At some point in this century, India will be the world's largest economy."

— Jeffrey Sachs, Columbia University economist

Asia as the center of gravity

Sachs framed his prediction within a broader historical shift. "The center of gravity of the world economy has moved back to Asia where it was for 2,000 years and then briefly departed after 1800. It's moved back to Asia," he said.

He identified the United States, China, India and Russia as the world's four major powers and said multipolarity is already an established reality rather than an aspiration. BRICS, which he said accounts for roughly 40% of the global economy, functions as a counterweight to unilateral decisions and military actions, he argued — a view he said was echoed in the joint declaration issued by BRICS countries in Delhi.

Criticism of Washington

Sachs was unsparing toward the Trump administration's trade policy, criticizing what he described as unilateral actions that disrupt the global order. His remarks follow the imposition of 50% US tariffs on Indian imports, a move he has previously called unconstitutional and counterproductive for India.

The economist has long argued that India's strategic future lies in economic engagement with China rather than in military alignment with the United States through the Quad. A strong India-China economic relationship, he said, would be "wonderful for India's economy" and essential to "building a multipolar world that isn't dependent on the US's whims."

Diaspora angle

For the Indian diaspora, Sachs' forecast is a reminder of where the long-term economic center of gravity is heading. NRIs allocating savings between India and the West are already betting on India's growth story — Sachs is effectively arguing that the demographic and economic arithmetic behind that bet is now a consensus among global economists, even as he urges deeper trade ties between the two Asian giants rather than the tariff wars of recent months.

What's next

The test of Sachs' thesis will play out over the coming years: whether India and China can manage their border tensions well enough to expand economic cooperation, and whether the BRICS framework delivers concrete alternatives to Western-dominated trade and finance architecture. The Delhi summit's joint declaration signaled political will, but converting that into technology partnerships, supply-chain integration and joint ventures is where the prediction will be proven or punctured.
